_about.rule: A verdict of keep, revise or remove rests on a source fetched on the date above (sourceUrl), or — only where the entry says so in `change` — on the product's own code read and run that day. Everything else is "unverified — needs a local clinician"; for those, `leaning` holds the direction a clinician is asked to confirm and is NOT a decision. Second pass: a row marked `recordOnly` is a record list or checklist with no formula, weight, cut-off, band, grade, interval or stage in its code; its verdict "keep — record list; wording for a local clinician" rests on the code read that day, and only its wording waits for a clinician.

SAFETY. (1) The referral flags are labelled "KDIGO criterion" but do not match the KDIGO 2024 list read today. KDIGO 2024 lists, among others: eGFR below 30; a sustained fall in GFR of more than 20%; albumin-to-creatinine ratio of 300 mg/g or more together with hematuria; a ratio consistently above 700 mg/g; a 5-year kidney-failure risk of 3 to 5% by a validated equation. The tool instead flags any ratio above 300 mg/g alone, a fall of more than 25% in a year, and "the very-high-risk cell" — the last is not on KDIGO's list at all. (2) With no albumin result typed, the tool still shows a risk colour, silently treating the patient as category A1: eGFR 75 with no urine test reads "Low risk (green cell)". The cell needs both values; with one missing the tool should show the GFR category only. (3) A ratio of exactly 300 mg/g is called A2; the two KDIGO/KDOQI texts read today write the severe category as "300 mg/g or more". The category table itself could not be read: a nephrologist settles the boundary. (4) The tool asks the doctor to type eGFR: add the US equation (CKD-EPI 2021, see the core set). Units (mg/g; mL/min/1.73 m²) are right for the US. Show it also to family medicine, endocrinology and cardiology. SECOND PASS. Point (3) is settled, and the code is right: Table 3 of the full KDIGO 2024 guideline, read today, puts A2 at 30 to 300 mg/g and A3 above 300 mg/g, which is what the code does (300 is A2); the GFR categories match its Table 2. The referral list was read again and the three faulty flags stand as described in (1). Licence: the guideline is published under a Creative Commons licence that allows neither commercial use nor adaptations, and requests to reproduce go to KDIGO.

tools.change: Second pass. FORMULA RIGHT, BANDS NOT SUPPORTED. The arithmetic in the code (four regions weighted 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 and 0.4; three signs scored 0 to 4; an area score of 0 to 6; total 0 to 72) matches the formula as printed in a drug-review report held by the US National Library of Medicine. Faults in the code, as in the first pass: a form with one box filled is scored as if every empty box were 0, and a score of 0 is called "Mild". Not opened: the 1978 publication (Fredriksson and Pettersson) and the text of the joint AAD–NPF guideline (the journal's site refused the fetch). A US dermatologist decides whether any band stays.

tools.change: Second pass. SAFETY — A WRONG SCORE FOR A CHILD UNDER 8. The instrument's own user guide gives two sets of region multipliers: for patients of 8 and over the ones the tool uses (head and neck 0.1, upper limbs 0.2, trunk 0.3, lower limbs 0.4), and for children under 8 another set (0.2, 0.2, 0.3, 0.3). The tool never asks the age and always uses the first set: a young child with severe eczema of the head and neck only (all four signs 3, area score 6) is given 7.2 where the guide's multiplier gives 14.4. Ask the age, or refuse a patient under 8. BANDS: the tool's three ("Mild below 7, Moderate 7 to 20.9, Severe 21 or above") are not the published strata read today (Leshem and colleagues, 2015: clear 0; almost clear 0.1 to 1.0; mild 1.1 to 7.0; moderate 7.1 to 21.0; severe 21.1 to 50.0; very severe 50.1 to 72.0). A score of 7.0 is shown as "Moderate" and 21.0 as "Severe" where the paper says mild and moderate; 0 is called "Mild"; there is no clear, almost clear or very severe step. Also: the guide allows half points (1.5 and 2.5) for a sign, and the tool takes whole numbers only. Right in the code: the four signs, the area table and the 0 to 72 range for a patient of 8 or over. The 2001 publication itself was not opened.

tools.change: MISLEADING HERE. The tool calls any average up to 25 dB "Within normal limits". The American Speech-Language-Hearing Association's table, from the very paper the tool cites (Clark 1981), has Normal up to 15 dB and a separate "Slight" loss from 16 to 25 dB: a 20 dB average is reported as normal where the US reference calls it a slight hearing loss (it matters most in children). Add the "Slight" grade. Not verified today: which frequencies make up the average in US practice (the tool uses 0.5, 1, 2 and 4 kHz), and the 10 dB and 15 dB flags. The audiologist role should see this tool too; today only otolaryngology does. SECOND PASS. (a) Confirmed on two more ASHA pages: the table of the paper the tool cites has the "Slight" step. (b) Frequencies: the National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders describes the speech-frequency average as 500, 1000 and 2000 Hz, and the four-frequency average of 500, 1000, 2000 and 4000 Hz — the one the tool uses — as the one of population studies; the same page treats averages of 25 dB or less as normal speech hearing. So two US conventions exist and the tool mixes them: four frequencies, a citation whose table has a slight step, bands without it. Say which average is shown and offer the three-frequency one. (c) Asymmetry: the otolaryngology academy's red-flag statement speaks of a difference of more than 15 dB between the ears; the tool flags at exactly 15 dB (an average of 30 dB against 15 dB in the other ear is flagged). (d) The 10 dB flag on the average is the tool's own: the federal workplace rule that uses 10 dB averages 2000, 3000 and 4000 Hz, not these frequencies.

tools.change: LICENCE AND LAW. Take the BI-RADS names off the screen until that agreement exists. The College's other reporting systems carry registered or claimed marks as well.
